newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Boom oil finds could be kept quiet in Australia.
newsitem.headline: Boom oil finds could be kept quiet in Australia.

text.p: Investors and analysts who expect to be among the first to know about the next large oil discovery off the Australian coast had better think again.

Waivers to listing rules recently granted by the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) to two of Australia's biggest oil producers and explorers, the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd and Santos Ltd, means a gusher will no longer be immediately reported.

Instead, shareholders, analysts and rival drillers might only find out what happened if the discovery is large enough to have a substantial impact on the share price of BHP or Santos. And given the size of the firms, the find would have to be big.

The issue of waivers is proving a headache for Australia's top oil producer group and for the stock exchange, which plans to call for public submissions into possible changes to the relevant listing rules.
INDUSTRY WOULD LIKE TO WAVE PROBLEM AWAY

The Australian Petroleum Production and Exploration Association (APPEA), which counts large and small local explorers plus international companies as members, has been asked by the stock exchange for advice on possible changes.
But APPEA first needs to develop its own coherent position and has released a discussion paper to member firms which shows the complexity of the issue.
Smaller APPEA members, who have lower market capitalisations and more problems raising capital for costly drilling adventures, want all discoveries publicised as they boost their share price.
The bigger the company, the less important this becomes.

Larger oil companies in general are also more loathe to release information about bigger prospects until they can buy up rights to land around their finds. Control of a wider area of oil-rich land can mean higher profits.
For oil industry analysts in Australia, the issue is about keeping the market, and their clients, informed.

"Australian investors are used to disclosure on a regular basis so anything where you suddenly have less disclosure is a cause for concern," said Dianne Brookman at Sydney broker Burdette Buckeridge and Young.
DRILLING NEAR INDONESIA IS KEY PART OF WAIVER
The waivers last until the end of June 1998 and apply to wells drilled in Zone of Cooperation (ZOCA) permits straddling Australia and Indonesia, as well as overseas wells.
BHP also received a waiver for two wells drilled in the Bass Strait oilfields, off the coast of Victoria, earlier this year.

The waivers allow BHP and Santos to bypass ASX listing rules which specify the need for progress reports on the status of each well, in particular items such as hydrocarbon shows, drilling depths and positioning.
Each argued successfully that the waivers are needed to protect their relationships with foreign partners who are not used to such stringent reports on their home turf.

"It is important for Australian companies to be involved in international activities and often the ground rules for those activities are different from the ones in Australia," said Santos corporate affairs manager Dr Graeme Bethune.
FOREIGN FIRMS BUY INTO AUSTRALIAN PERMITS
While Australia is not in the big league of oil production, the country produces about 500,000 barrels a day, with about 40 percent of that from the Bass Strait fields operated by Exxon Corp
A number of United States explorers, attracted in particular by the prospectivity of the Timor Sea region which includes ZOCA, have taken significant stakes in some permits.
These companies include Phillips Petroleum, Mobil Corp, and Chevron Corp

Another listing rule also has the potential to force the public release of information about a well. This rule becomes effective if the information can have a "material" effect on the company's share price.
But as there is no official definition of "material", this means that at the end of the day it is up to the company to decide if the information has to be released to the market.

"They have only got waivers where it doesn't impact on the shares. BHP understands that," said ASX companies officer Tim Jess. "The reality is with BHP what sort of well would impact on the shares? It is a pretty big company and petroleum is only one division," Jess said.
A QUESTION OF SCALE

With a market capitalisation of A$37.8 billion (US$29.11 billion) and a share price of more than A$19, few wells would have an obvious impact on BHP's share price. At A$5.57 per share and a valuation of A$3.0 billion, the same probably applies to Santos.
"Material information tends to be immaterial to big companies, you could argue that 20-30 cents on BHP's share price is immaterial," said the chief executive of one foreign-owned producer.
"For smaller companies, some of them don't have share prices worth 20 or 30 cents so you know it is hugely significant and material and they would want to continue to report every nuance," he said.

To be fair, information about ZOCA wells is released in quick detail at the moment as neither BHP nor Santos own the permits outright and are in partnership with smaller locals who file their own drilling reports.
SMALL EXPLORERS COULD FIND PROBLEM COSTLY

But it is the divergent views of the big and small explorers which could eventually lead to an industry-wide split over waivers, one chief executive told Reuters. "It is the smaller companies which are going to suffer in the long run," he said, explaining that they could become less attractive partners.
"They will get short term gains by being able to make these announcements, but in future times when large companies are looking for partners the smaller companies will find it very difficult."
(A$1 = 77 US cents)
